chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from some of his companions, from Ibrahim ibn Abi al-Bilad, from the one who mentioned it, he said:

Luqman (peace be upon him) said to his son: 'O my dear son! Do not draw too near, lest you become more distant; and do not be too remote, lest you be humiliated. Every creature loves its own kind, and indeed the son of Adam loves his fellow human.

Do not display your goods except to one who seeks them. Just as there is no friendship between the wolf and the ram, similarly there is no friendship between the righteous and the immoral. Whoever draws near to tar, some of it will stick to him; similarly, whoever associates with an immoral person will learn from his ways.

Whoever loves disputation will be insulted; whoever enters the haunts of evil will be accused; whoever keeps company with an evil companion will not remain safe; and whoever does not control his tongue will regret it.'

key_terms.البَارّ: The pious/righteous person; one who fulfills obligations toward God and family
key_terms.الزِّفت: Tar, pitch or asphalt; used metaphorically for moral contamination through association
key_terms.الفاجر: The immoral/wicked person; one who openly transgresses moral and religious boundaries
key_terms.المِرَاء: Disputation, contentious argumentation; condemned as leading to insult and social harm
key_terms.خُلَّة: Intimate friendship, a deep bond of companionship; stronger than ordinary friendship

ai.seo_question: What did Luqman advise his son about choosing companions and social relations?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, Luqman (AS) — the wise man mentioned in the Quran — advises his son on social conduct and companionship. The advice addresses the golden mean in social relations: neither excessive familiarity nor excessive distance. The central teaching warns against associating with the immoral (al-fajir) through a vivid analogy of tar sticking to whoever touches it, reflecting the ancient wisdom tradition that character is shaped by one's companions. The original audience, early Muslim scholars of the 3rd century AH, would have recognized these as principles of character formation (tarbiyah) in a community still negotiating the norms of Islamic social ethics.
word_analysis: its seeker/the one who needs it
